Common collaboration problems

Overwritten files

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
What Is an Issue?
Issues = structured project tasks
Examples:

Fix species names
Update occupancy model
Add metadata documentation
Review extraction decisions
Improve README

Issues make work visible.

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Why Issues Matter
Issues help teams:

Track progress
Document decisions
Clarify responsibilities
Discuss problems transparently
Reduce invisible work

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Example issue
Issue #14
Add metadata documentation for camera trap dataset
Possible discussion:

What needs to be done?
Who is responsible?
When is it complete?

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Clone vs Fork vs Branch
All three involve “copies” in some way.
But they happen at different levels:



Concept
Happens where?
Purpose




Clone
Your computer
Download repo locally


Branch
Inside repository
Safe parallel work


Fork
On GitHub
Your own copy of another repo

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Cloning a Repository
Clone = download repository locally
You use clone when you want to:

work on a project
run analyses
edit files locally
connect GitHub to RStudio

Example https://github.com/DrMattG/Open_wildlife_workshop.git
Now the project exists on your computer.

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Visual Clone Diagram
GitHub repository

        ↓ clone

Your computer

        ↓

Local editable project

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
What Is a Branch?
Branches = safe experimentation
A branch is:
a parallel version inside a repository used for development and testing isolated from the main workflow

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Branch Workflow Diagram
main
 ├── fix-readme
 ├── occupancy-update
 └── new-figures
Each branch can evolve independently.

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Why Branches Matter
Branches are useful for:

Testing new analyses
Trying ideas safely
Collaborative editing
Reviewing changes
Protecting stable workflows

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Pull Requests
A pull request means:

“Please review my changes before merging them.”

PRs support:

Review
Discussion
Transparency
Quality control

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Pull Request Workflow
Create issue
      ↓
Create branch
      ↓
Make changes
      ↓
Commit changes
      ↓
Open pull request
      ↓
Review + discussion
      ↓
Merge into main

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Forking Workflow Example
Example contribution workflow
Original repository
        ↓
Fork repository
        ↓
Clone fork locally
        ↓
Create branch
        ↓
Make changes
        ↓
Push branch
        ↓
Open pull request

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
When Would You Fork?
Forks are useful when:

contributing to external projects
collaborating across organisations
teaching workflows
experimenting independently
contributing to open-source tools

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Common Fears
“This seems complicated”
Reality:

Most workflows are small
Mistakes are common
Nobody learns Git perfectly immediately

The goal is reducing chaos, not perfection.

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Editing directly on main
Problem:

unstable workflows
accidental breakage
difficult recovery

Better:

use branches for changes

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Giant commits
Bad:
Update everything
Better:
Add occupancy model script

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Small commits are easier to:

understand
review
reverse

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Documentation
Without documentation:

onboarding becomes difficult
workflows become fragile
collaborators get lost

README files matter.

title: Collaboration Workflows
section: Project knowledge trapped in one person
text:
Project knowledge trapped in one person
Danger signs:

“Only Alex knows how this works”
undocumented scripts
unclear setup instructions
mysterious folders

Good workflows reduce dependency on individuals.

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Project Handover
Projects should survive turnover

students graduate
staff change jobs
collaborations evolve
projects pause and restart

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Helpful project features

README
clear folder structure
setup instructions
metadata
reproducible scripts
documented decisions
version control history

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:

In pairs:

Create an issue
Create a branch

Review and merge

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Merge Conflicts
Merge conflicts happen
Conflict means:
Two changes affect the same lines.

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Important
Conflicts are:

normal
solvable
not catastrophic

title: Collaboration Workflows
text:
Collaboration Is Infrastructure
Good workflows help:

Reduce stress
Reduce errors
Improve continuity
Improve transparency
Improve collaboration
Improve science

title: GitHub without fear
section: Open workflows for ecology and wildlife research
text:
Open workflows for ecology and wildlife research
Topics:

Repositories
Commits

README files

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Learning Goals
By the end of this session you should be able to:

Understand what Git and GitHub are
Create and clone repositories
Make commits confidently
Push and pull changes

title: GitHub without fear
text:
What Problem Does Git Solve?
A familiar workflow problem
analysis_final.R
analysis_final_v2.R
analysis_final_v2_REAL.R
analysis_final_USE_THIS_ONE.R

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Common issues

Files overwritten
Unsure what changed
Difficult collaboration
No backup history
Impossible to undo mistakes safely

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Git is not GitHub
Git

Version control system
Tracks changes to files
Works locally on your computer

GitHub

Online hosting platform for Git repositories
Collaboration and sharing
Backup and project management

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Version control
Git keeps a history of changes:

What changed
When it changed
Who changed it
Why it changed

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Benefits

Undo mistakes
Track project history
Collaborate safely
Experiment without fear

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Why GitHub Matters in Ecology
Ecology is collaborative
Examples:

Multi-author papers
Monitoring projects
Shared codebases
Long-term projects
Student supervision
Evidence synthesis workflows

title: GitHub without fear
text:
What Is a Repository?
Repository = project folder + history
A repository contains:

Code
Data (although it shouldn’t)
Documentation
Figures
Workflow history

Think of it as:
A project folder with memory.

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Commits
Commits are snapshots
A commit records:

What changed
When it changed
A short explanation

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Good commit messages
Add cleaning script for camera trap data
Fix species names in processed dataset

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Bad commit messages
stuff
asdfgh

title: GitHub without fear
text:
A Helpful Mental Model
Edit files
    ↓
Review changes
    ↓
Commit changes
    ↓
Push to GitHub

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Push and Pull
Push
Send your local commits to GitHub.
Pull
Download changes from GitHub.

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Typical workflow
Pull
Work
Commit
Push

title: GitHub without fear
text:
GitHub is useful for:

Backup
Project sharing
Collaboration (even with youself)
Public documentation
Teaching
Open science portfolios

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Common Fear #1
“What if I break everything?”
Good news:
Git is designed to:

Track changes
Recover mistakes
Restore earlier versions

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Mistakes are normal.
Even experienced users regularly:

Commit the wrong file
Merge incorrectly
Forget to pull

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Common Fear #2
“I don’t understand branches”
That is okay.
Branches come later…
You do not need to master Git immediately.

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Common Fear #3
“The terminal is scary”
Yes it is! You can do a lot using:

RStudio Git pane
GitHub Desktop
VS Code interfaces

Understanding concepts matters more than memorising commands.

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Common Mistakes
Common “beginner” mistakes

Forgetting to commit
Committing large files
Editing directly on GitHub accidentally
Conflicts after forgetting to pull
Uploading sensitive data

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Guided practice
You will:

Create a GitHub repository
Connect it to RStudio
Add your reproducible project
Commit changes
Push to GitHub
Edit README
Pull updates

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Create a GitHub repository
On GitHub:

Click “New repository”
Choose a repository name
Add a README
Set visibility
Create repository

Suggested name:
wildlife-reproducibility-workshop

title: GitHub without fear
text:
“Clone” repository into RStudio
In RStudio:
File → New Project → Version Control → Git
Paste repository URL.

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Result
You now have:

Local repository
Git tracking enabled
GitHub connection established

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Add project files
Copy into the repository:

data_raw/
scripts/
outputs/
README.md

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Observe Git pane
RStudio now shows changed files.

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Make your first commit
In Git pane:

Tick changed files
Click “Commit”
Write message

Example:
Add initial project structure and scripts

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Push to GitHub
Click:
Push

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Refresh GitHub page
Your project is now online.

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Edit the README
Add:

Project description
Your name
Workshop details
Folder explanation

Commit and push changes.

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Important habits

Always pull before starting work.
Commit often

title: GitHub without fear
text:
Be careful with:

Sensitive species locations
Confidential data
Personal information
Large raw files
Passwords/API keys

What Quarto Does
Quarto combines:

Narrative text
R code
Figures
Tables

Into one reproducible document.

Data 
↓ 
Scripts 
↓ 
Quarto document 
↓

Parameterised reports

multiple species reports
multiple site reports
multiple years
multiple regions

Automatically.
